en: Var-v § 0 – Var-v § 1 – Var-v § 1.1.a: The Buddha, the Blessed One, entered the rains retreat at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada.
Var-v § 1.1.b–c:
The Blessed One said: "Therefore, I authorize that a monk should enter the rains retreat.
Var-v § 1.2: It was stated by the Blessed One that a monk should enter the rains retreat. The monks did not know how the rains retreat should be entered.
The Blessed One said: ... [Var-v § 1.2.1] ...
Thereafter, a monk who is to be appointed as the distributor of bedding and seats (*śayanāsanagrāhaka*) should be selected.
[Var-v § 1.2.2] A monk endowed with five qualities who has not been appointed as the distributor of bedding and seats should not be appointed.

And one who is approved should be appointed. By which five [qualities]? He acts out of desire, he acts out of hatred, he acts out of delusion, he acts out of fear, and he does not know whether bedding and seating have been assigned or not. A monk endowed with these five qualities, even if unappointed as a distributor of bedding and seating, should not be appointed.
And once appointed, he should not be dismissed.

Var-v § 1.2.2.b A monk endowed with five qualities who has not been appointed as a distributor of lodgings (*śayanāsana-grāhaka*) should be appointed; and once appointed, he should not be dismissed. What are these five?
He does not act out of favoritism (*chandāt*).
He does not go [to accept lodgings] out of hatred, nor out of delusion, nor out of fear;

he knows whether bedding and seating have been assigned or not yet assigned. A monk endowed with these five qualities who has not been appointed as the distributor of bedding and seating should be appointed, and once appointed, he should not be dismissed.
Furthermore, he should be authorized in this manner: having prepared the seating and bedding,
struck the ghaṇṭā, and questioned the monks by means of a formal inquiry, when the entire Saṃgha has sat down and assembled, he should first be encouraged [to undertake the task].

"Are you, [Name], able to cause the Saṃgha to accept the summer bedding and seating? He should reply, "I am able. Thereafter, one monk, having made a formal motion (*jñapti*), should perform the ritual act (*karman*).
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha. This monk named so-and-so, the distributor of lodgings, is capable of distributing the Saṃgha’s lodgings for the rainy season.

If it seems timely to the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha permit and authorize that the Saṃgha appoint this monk named so-and-so as the distributor of lodgings; the monk named so-and-so, as the distributor of lodgings, shall distribute the Saṃgha’s lodgings for the rainy season. This is the motion."
Var-v § 1.2.5 And thus the ritual action (karman) should be performed:

"May the venerable Saṃgha listen. The monk named so-and-so, the distributor of lodgings and seats, is capable of distributing the Saṃgha’s lodgings and seats for the rainy season retreat. Therefore, let the Saṃgha appoint the monk named so-and-so as the distributor of lodgings and seats."
This monk, named so-and-so, shall be the assigner of lodgings for the Sangha during the rainy season retreat.
Those venerable ones who consent to appoint this monk, named so-and-so, as the assigner of lodgings, let them remain silent; those who do not consent, let them speak.

The Saṃgha has approved the monk named so-and-so as the distributor of lodgings and seats. He shall distribute the Saṃgha’s lodgings and seats for the rainy season retreat. It is accepted and authorized by the Saṃgha, since there is silence;
thus do I hold it to be so.
Var-v § 1.2.6: I shall prescribe the rules of customary conduct for the monk who is assigned to provide bedding and seating.

Thereafter, the formal agreement (*kriyākāra*) should be announced: "Listen, venerable Saṃgha! In this residence, there is this and that formal agreement. Whoever among you is able to enter the rains-retreat according to this and that formal agreement, let him take a voting stick (*śalākā*). And no monk among you..."
"In this year... whoever among you knows anything [of this matter], let him speak now.
Let him not cause a dispute later during the rainy season. The Saṃgha will consider that he who causes a dispute among you during the rainy season must be further examined."

Thereafter, the monk serving as the distributor of bedding and seats (*śayanāsanagrāhaka*) should distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*). [The senior monk] should cause the voting sticks of the Teacher to be taken first. Thereafter, the elder of the Saṃgha (*saṃghasthavira*), having left half the seat vacant, should take a voting stick and place it down slowly. This should continue in the same manner down to the youngest member of the Saṃgha (*saṃghanavaka*). For the novices (*śrāmaṇera*), their preceptors (*ācārya*) and instructors (*upādhyāya*) [should do so].
The voting sticks (*śalākā*) should be distributed. Thereafter, one should count them, noting: "In this residence, voting sticks have been taken by so many monks.

Then, after that, the monk appointed as the distributor of bedding and seats (*śayanāsana-grāhaka*), taking the key and the tally-stick (*tāḍaka*), should stand before the senior of the Saṃgha and say: "Venerable Sir, such-and-such a monastery has gains."
[He is] one who possesses a robe. "Take it. If he takes it, that which was the dwelling of the senior of the Saṃgha must be given to the second senior.
If the senior of the Saṃgha does not take it, it must be given to the second senior.

The second elder shall not accept it; it should be given to the third elder. If it has been accepted by the third elder and the elder of the Saṃgha requests it, it shall not be given at the first request. It shall not be given at the second request. At the third request, it shall be given. [This applies to] the elder of the Saṃgha.

And he must confess his offense as a *duṣkṛta* that transgresses the discipline. In this manner, up until the case where he is selected by the junior-most member of the Saṃgha: if the third junior-most member of the Saṃgha requests [the selection], it should not be granted on the first utterance; it should not be granted on the second utterance; it should be granted on the third utterance. And the third junior-most member of the Saṃgha must likewise confess his offense as a *duṣkṛta* that transgresses the discipline.

Var-v § 1.3.1: The monks assigned all the monasteries [to specific individuals]. Consequently, visiting monks were inconvenienced. The Blessed One said: "For the sake of visiting monks, there should be a place not assigned. Var-v § 1.3.2: The monks even assigned [places] in the gate-houses. The Blessed One said: "One must not assign [places] in the gate-house."
The monks designated palaces as places to dwell. The Blessed One said, "One should not designate a palace [as a dwelling].
In palaces that were uninhabited, crows, sparrows, and pigeons made their home. The Blessed One said:

A monk should be appointed as the guardian of the storehouse (peḍavārika). He must inspect it. If the eggs have not yet hatched, they should be removed; if they have hatched, they should be left alone. The *tryaṃbuka* and *trailāṭa* [insects] dwell there. The Blessed One said:
One should examine them. If the eggs have not been released, they should be removed. Or, if they have been released, one should tie a thread [around them], thinking, "They will not undergo growth."
Thereafter, bedding and seating should be given.
If there are few items, one should be given to each; or if there are many, [they should be distributed accordingly].
Two or two, or three or three, should be given;
there are other large items [to be provided],
and the very elderly monks are becoming exhausted by the labor of preparing them.
The Blessed One said:
"They should be given to those who have relied upon them.

Thereafter, the monk who takes charge of the lodgings and seats must announce the formal agreement (*kriyākāra*): "No monk whatsoever shall [use] the communal lodging and seat without a covering cloth (*pratyāstarana*)."

It should not be used with a mat made of strips of cloth, nor with a thick blanket, nor with a single-layered garment, nor with a double-layered garment. If one should use the bedding and seating belonging to the Saṅgha while it is not yet permitted for use,
the Saṅgha will consider that person to be subject to further investigation.

Var-v § 1.6.2: A monk who is in charge of lodgings must inspect the lodgings every half-month. If he sees that the lodgings are worn out through lack of use, he should announce it to the Saṃgha and have them repaired. Alternatively, if they are new, he should announce it to his preceptors and teachers and have them repaired.
Var-v § 1.7.1: After that, he should announce it to the assembly: "Tomorrow the Saṃgha will enter the rains retreat in such-and-such a village for alms."
Var-v § 1.7.2 Thereafter, having surveyed the dwelling and the alms-round, and having entered a secluded place, the rains should be entered.

Var-v § 1.7.2.a How is the dwelling to be surveyed? One should consider: "Will there be wise fellow-practitioners in this place who will not cause unarisen suffering and dejection to arise, nor [allow] arisen [suffering and dejection to persist]?"
And they will quickly dispel [those afflictions],

and they will think that they shall produce happiness and mental joy that have not yet arisen, and shall properly and thoroughly protect that which has already arisen; or, for one who is ill, there shall be an attendant.

In this way, the residence should be inspected. (Var-v § 1.7.2.b) How should the alms-round be inspected? One should consider: "Will there be givers of alms-food for me in this village or its vicinity? And will there be givers of medicine for one who is ill?"
In this way, the proper sphere of conduct (*gocara*) should be observed.

Thereafter, having entered a sheltered place, having performed the formal salutation (*sāmīcī*) according to seniority toward the monks, having squatted down (*utkuṭuka*), and having raised his joined palms (*añjali*), he should speak as follows:
"Pay attention, Venerable One! Today is the *Kāṣāḍhī* [full moon], the commencement of the rainy season retreat for the Saṃgha... I, that very person..."

"I, [name], in this residence within the boundary, enter upon the rains for the preceding three-month period, with such-and-such a service-provider and such-and-such a village for alms, solely for the purpose of repairing what is broken and dilapidated in this residence. Here are my rains;
here is my residence for the rains. Thus a second time.
Thus three times.
Monks, the rains-retreat must be entered;
furthermore, a monk who has observed the rains-retreat must not go outside the boundary.
If he goes, he must not dwell there.
It was said by the Blessed One: "A monk who has completed the rains retreat must not go outside the boundary. If he goes, he must not dwell there.
In the village of Hastibāla, there lived a householder named Udayana; his household and family...

A personal invitation had been presented to him. Consequently, he had gathered there a great abundance of robes and material offerings. He dispatched a messenger to the monks, saying, "May the venerable ones come; they shall partake [of the offerings]. The monks began to inquire: "How far away is Hastibālagrāmaka? "It is more than three yojanas. "We will be able to go and return this very day; we will not be able [to do so]."
They reflected:
"The Blessed One has declared that a monk who has entered the rains retreat must not go outside the boundary. If he does go, he must not dwell there. Thus, they did not go.
However, those monks who had entered the rains retreat in the vicinity of Hastibālagrāma were provided with an abundance of robes and material offerings.

After the passing of those three months of the rainy season, having finished their robes and completed their sewing, they took up their bowls and outer robes and set out on a walking tour toward Śrāvastī. Traveling by stages on their tour, they arrived at Śrāvastī. When the monks saw them from afar, they addressed them: (76r = GBM 734)

"Welcome, welcome, venerable ones! You have been refreshed; you have been addressed. From where, venerable ones, do you come now? Or where did you spend the rains? "We have come from Hastibālagrāmaka, venerable ones;
we spent the rains in Hastibālagrāmaka. "I trust, venerable ones, that you spent the rains in Hastibālagrāmaka in comfort and ease?"
"Or were you not exhausted by the alms-food? "It is true, Venerable Ones, that we spent the rains comfortably in the village of Hastibāla;
we were not exhausted by the alms-food.
"In what way, Venerable Ones, did you spend the rains comfortably in the village of Hastibāla?"

Nor were you exhausted for lack of almsfood. There, in the village of Hastibāla, there lived a householder named Udayana. His household was well-provided for and he had ample means at his disposal; he bestowed upon us a great abundance of clothing and material gifts. Thus, venerable sirs, we have spent the rains in the village of Hastibāla in comfort and ease.
"We have stayed here, yet we have not been weary for lack of alms.

They said, "Venerable ones, that householder has also sent a messenger to us, saying, 'May the noble ones come; you shall partake of food. We asked him, 'How far is Hastibālagrāmaka? He replied, 'More than [one yojana]..."

[We were] three *yojanas* away. Then this thought occurred to us: "The Blessed One has said that a monk who has entered the rains retreat must not go outside the boundary; if he does go, he must not dwell there. We did not go. The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One reflected: "Alas, my disciples desire acquisitions of robes and acquisitions of food. What if I were to authorize the monks to remain for seven days for the sake of dwelling in comfort and for the sake of the donors' enjoyment of the gift? Therefore, I authorize that one may go on business after having resolved [to stay] for seven days."

It was stated by the Blessed One in Var-v § 1.8.2: "Having empowered oneself for seven days, one may go on account of business. The monks did not know what kind of business it was. Regarding this matter, the Blessed One said to the monks:

"On account of the business of a layman (*upāsaka*), on account of the business of a laywoman (*upāsikā*), on account of the business of a monk (*bhikṣu*), on account of the business of a nun (*bhikṣuṇī*), a female trainee (*śikṣamāṇā*), a male novice (*śrāmaṇeraka*), or a female novice (*śrāmaṇerikā*)."

Var-v § 1.8.2.1.1: What is to be done by a lay follower (*upāsaka*)? Suppose there is a lay follower for whom a household project has arisen that requires his own personal involvement. He has there accumulated a great abundance of clothing and material gains. He sends a messenger to the monks, saying: "May the noble ones come; they shall partake [of these things]."

A monk may go for seven days, having made a formal determination, on account of a business matter for a lay follower (*upāsaka*). This is what constitutes a business matter for a lay follower. Furthermore, there is another business matter for a lay follower: namely, when a lay follower wishes to establish a monastery for the Saṅgha of monks from the four directions, he provides there a great abundance of clothing and requisites.
And material gain has been acquired. He sends a messenger to the monks, saying, "May the noble ones come; they shall partake [of the food].

A monk may go for seven days, having made a formal determination (*adhiṣṭhāya*), for the sake of a lay follower's business. This is the business of a lay follower. Furthermore, there is another business of a lay follower: namely, when a lay follower in that [place]...

He desires to provide bedding and seating in that monastery. Consequently, he has procured there an abundance of acquisitions of robes and acquisitions of food. He sends a messenger to the monks, saying: "May the noble ones come; they shall enjoy [these things].
A monk may go for seven days after having made a formal determination (*adhiṣṭhāna*) on account of a task for a lay follower (*upāsaka*). This is the task for a lay follower.

Furthermore, there is another duty for a lay follower (*upāsaka*). Suppose that a lay follower wishes to establish a permanent provision of alms-food (*dhruvabhikṣā*) in that very monastery as a favorable offering (*anukūlayajña*). Consequently, a great abundance of clothing and material gains (*āmiṣalābha*) has been accumulated there. He then sends a messenger to the monks.
"May the noble ones come; they will partake [of the meal]. A monk may go for seven days after having made a formal resolve (*adhiṣṭhāya*) on account of a duty for a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
This is the duty of a lay follower.
Furthermore, there is another duty of a lay follower: namely, when a lay follower desires to have the body of the Tathāgata or a stūpa established in that very monastery.

He sends a messenger to the monks, saying: "May the noble ones come; they will be companions in the Dharma. A monk may go for seven days, having made a formal determination, for the sake of a lay follower's business. This is the lay follower's business.

Furthermore, there is another business of a lay follower: namely, when a lay follower performs the raising of a staff, the raising of a parasol, the raising of a banner, or the raising of a flag upon that very stūpa.

He wishes to provide anointing with oil, anointing with sandalwood, and anointing with saffron. He sends a messenger to the monks, saying, "May the noble ones come; they shall be my companions in the Dharma. A monk may go for the sake of a lay follower's business, having authorized himself for seven days. This is the business of a lay follower.

Var-v § 1.8.2.1.7 Furthermore, there is another duty for a lay follower (*upāsaka*). It is as follows: suppose one of the four collections of discourses (*sūtranikāya*) has been extensively taught and promulgated by a lay follower, and through that, a great abundance of acquisitions of robes and material goods has been gathered there. He [should give them] to the monks...

He sends a messenger: "May the noble ones come; they shall partake [of the meal]. A monk may go for seven days after having made a formal determination (adhiṣṭhāya) for the sake of a lay follower's business. This is the lay follower's business.
Furthermore, there is another lay follower's business: namely, when a lay follower has remorse (kaukṛtya).

It arises. He sends a messenger to the monks, saying, "May the venerable ones come; they shall dispel the remorse that has arisen. A monk may go for seven days, having made a formal determination, on account of a task for a lay follower.
This is the task for a lay follower.

Var-v § 1.8.2.1.9 Furthermore, there is another duty for a lay follower (*upāsaka*). Suppose a harmful view (*pāpaka-dṛṣṭigata*) has arisen in a lay follower; he sends a messenger to the monks, saying, "May the venerable ones come, so that they may cause me to relinquish this harmful view that has arisen. A monk must go, having authorized himself for seven days.
This is what must be done by a lay follower (*upāsaka*). This is the duty of a lay follower.
Furthermore, there is another duty of a lay follower: namely, when the Saṃgha intends to overturn the alms-bowl (*pātra*) of a lay follower, he sends a messenger to the monks.

"Let the noble ones come; they will take their side according to the Dharma. A monk may go for seven days after having made a formal determination (*adhiṣṭhāya*) for the sake of a lay follower’s business. This is the business of a lay follower.

Furthermore, there is another business of a lay follower: namely, when a bowl has been turned upside down by the Saṃgha against a lay follower, he sends a messenger to the monks, saying, "Let the noble ones come; [the bowl]..."
"You shall cause him who is submerged to emerge.
A monk may go for seven days, having made a formal determination (*adhiṣṭhāya*), on account of a duty for a lay follower (*upāsaka*). This is a duty for a lay follower.
Furthermore, there is another duty for a lay follower: namely, when a lay follower is afflicted by illness...

He is suffering and severely ill. He sends a messenger to the monks, saying: "May the venerable ones come; they will give me their word. A monk may go for seven days, having formally resolved to do so, on account of a task for a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
This is what constitutes a task for a lay follower.
What is a task for a female lay follower (*upāsikā*)? It is setting aside household chores and weaving for oneself.

What is to be done by a monk? It is as follows: a monk may wish to offer a monastery to the Saṃgha of monks from the four quarters. He has there gathered a great abundance of acquisitions of robes and acquisitions of food.
He sends a messenger to the monks, saying: "Let the Venerable Ones come; they shall enjoy [these things]."

A monk may go away for seven days after having made a formal determination (*adhiṣṭhāya*), provided there is business for a monk. This is what constitutes "business for a monk. Furthermore, there is another kind of business for a monk:

namely, when a monk [must attend to] the monastery in that very same ārāma, his bedding and seats, the regular alms-food, the body of the Tathāgata, or a stūpa, or the consecration ceremony (*alaṃseka*).

When a monk has anointed himself with sandalwood paste, raised a staff, raised a banner, or recited one or another of the collections of discourses (*sūtrapiṭaka*), and a wicked state of remorse or an evil view arises within him, he sends a messenger to the monks, saying: "Let the venerable ones come;
they will cause me to relinquish this wicked view that has arisen. A monk must go [to them].
Having empowered it for seven days for the sake of a monk’s business. This is a monk’s business. Everything should be recited in detail as before.

Furthermore, there is another duty for a monk. It is as follows: when the Saṃgha wishes to perform such formal acts (*praṇidhi-karma*) against a monk, namely—the act of censure (*tarjanīya-karma*), the act of reprimand (*nigarhaṇīya-karma*), the act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karma*), the act of reconciliation (*pratisaṃharaṇīya-karma*), the act of suspension for not seeing [one's offense] (*adarśanāyotkṣepaṇīya-karma*), the act of suspension for not making amends (*apratikarmaṇāyotkṣepaṇīya-karma*), or [the act of suspension] for not relinquishing [an evil view] (*apratiniḥsṛṣṭe*).

Regarding a case involving an evil view, a formal act of suspension (*utkṣepaṇīya-karman*) is to be performed. He sends a messenger to the monks, saying: "Let the venerable ones come; they shall join the side that acts according to the Dharma. A monk may go for seven days, having made a formal determination, on account of a necessary business for a monk.
This is what constitutes a monk’s necessary business.

Furthermore, there is another duty for a monk. It is as follows: when the Saṃgha has performed such formal acts of resolution against a monk, namely—the act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*), the act of reprimand (*nigarhaṇīya-karman*), the act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), the act of reconciliation (*pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman*), the act of suspension for not seeing [one's offense], and the act of suspension for not making amends.
When a monk has not relinquished a wicked view, a formal act of suspension (utkṣepaṇīya-karman) is to be performed against him. He sends a messenger to the monks, saying:
"Venerable ones, please come; they will reinstate me. A monk must go for a period of seven days on account of a necessary business for a monk.
This is what constitutes a "necessary business for a monk."
Furthermore, there is another duty for a monk. Suppose a monk becomes afflicted, suffering, and severely ill;

he sends a messenger to the monks, saying, "May the Venerable Ones come and speak with me. A monk may go for seven days, having resolved upon it, for the sake of a monk's duty. This is the duty for a monk. What is the duty for a nun? [It is] excluding the acts of formal resolution (*praṇidhi-karman*).
Var-v § 1.8.2.4.2 – Var-v § 1.8.2.5.1: What is to be done by a female trainee (*śikṣamāṇā*)? All this very same [duty] is to be done by a female trainee. Var-v § 1.8.2.5.2:
Furthermore, there is another duty to be done by a female trainee. Namely, that a female trainee...

After two years, having trained in the six rules and the six secondary rules, she becomes one who has completed her training. She sends a messenger to the monks, saying: "May the noble ones come; they will confer full ordination. A monk may go for seven days, having authorized himself, on account of a necessary business for a *śikṣamāṇā*. This is the necessary business for a *śikṣamāṇā*.
Var-v § 1.8.2.6.1 What is to be done by a *śrāmaṇeraka*? All of this very same [set of duties] is to be done by a *śrāmaṇeraka*.

Var-v § 1.8.2.6.2 Furthermore, there is another duty to be performed by a *śrāmaṇeraka*: namely, when a *śrāmaṇeraka* has reached twenty years of age, he sends a messenger to the monks, saying, "May the venerable ones come; they will confer full ordination. A monk must go for seven days at most on account of the duty of a *śrāmaṇeraka*. This is the duty of a *śrāmaṇeraka*.

Var-v § 1.8.2.7.1 What is to be done by a female novice (śrāmaṇerikā)? All this very same [duty] is to be done by a female novice. Var-v § 1.8.2.7.2 Furthermore, there is another duty to be performed by a female novice:
namely, that a female novice who has lived at home for twelve years—
Or [she may be] one who has been a maiden for eighteen years. She sends a messenger to the monks, saying:

"May the noble ones come; for two years they will grant instruction in the six rules and the six secondary rules. A monk must go for seven days, having made a formal resolve, for the sake of a novice nun's business.
This is the business of a novice nun.
Var-v § 2: Summary Verse (uddāna).
Medicine, an attendant, men, women, and eunuchs;
signs, treasures, and kinsmen—on account of these obstacles, one may depart.
Var-v § 2.1.1: It may happen that a monk who has entered the rains retreat thinks to himself:

"I have entered the rains retreat in this residence, yet there is no one to give me almsfood. Not obtaining almsfood, I might become exhausted or even die; that would be an obstacle for me in attaining what I have not yet attained."
"For the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained, for the sake of realizing what has not yet been realized—
what if I were now to depart from this residence? Having departed from that residence, making this very circumstance the reason, there is no offense regarding the interruption of the rains retreat.

Var-v § 2.1.2: Furthermore, it may happen that a monk who has entered the rains retreat thinks to himself: "I have entered the rains retreat in this residence, yet there is no one to provide me with medicine for the sick when I am ill. Not obtaining medicine, I might suffer or even die. This would be an obstacle for me in attaining what I have not yet attained."

"For the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained, and for the sake of realizing what has not yet been realized—what if I were to depart from this residence? He departs from that residence. Making this very reason his justification, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains retreat.

Var-v § 2.1.3: It may happen that a monk who has entered the rains retreat thinks: "I have entered the rains retreat in this residence, yet I have no one to attend to me when I am ill. Because of being without an attendant, I might suffer or even die; that would be an obstacle for me in attaining what has not yet been attained."
"For the sake of attaining what has not yet been attained, for the sake of realizing what has not yet been realized—
what if I were to depart from this residence? Having departed from that residence on account of this very reason, there is no offense regarding the interruption of the rainy season retreat.

Varṣav § 2.1.4: It may happen that a woman approaches a monk who has entered the rains retreat and invites him with an improper invitation: "Stay here, Noble One! Enjoy yourself, Noble One! I will attend to you; I will give you my daughter, I will give you my daughter-in-law, I will give you my female slave, or I will give you my servant."
In that regard, a monk who has entered the rains retreat thinks:

"I have entered the rains retreat in this residence, and this woman approaches me and invites me with an improper invitation: 'Venerable sir, stay! Venerable sir, enjoy yourself! I shall attend to you; I will give you my daughter, or I will give you my daughter-in-law.'"

"I will give you a female slave, I will give you a laborer, I will give you a servant. If I were to spend the rains retreat in this residence, it would result for me in a threat to my life, a threat to my state of a recluse, and a threat to my holy life. What if I were to depart from this residence? He [departed] from there.
If one departs from the residence, making this very circumstance the reason, there is no offense regarding the interruption of the rains retreat.
Var-v § 2.1.5: Suppose that a man approaches a monk who has entered the rains retreat and invites him with an improper invitation:
"Stay, Noble One! Enjoy yourself, Noble One! I will give you my daughter; I will give you my daughter-in-law; I will give you my female slave; I will give you my laborer.
Then it occurs to that monk who has entered the rains retreat: "I have entered the rains retreat in this residence. This..."

And a man approached me and invited me with an improper invitation: "Stay, noble sir! Delight yourself, noble sir! I will give you my daughter; I will give you my daughter-in-law; I will give you a female slave; I will give you a laborer. [He thought: "If I were to dwell in this residence for the rains, it would lead to an obstacle to my life, an obstacle to my state of a recluse, and an obstacle to my holy life."
"What if I were to depart from this residence? He departs from that residence. Having made this very condition, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains retreat.
Var-v § 2.1.6: Suppose that a paṇḍaka approaches a monk who has entered the rains retreat and invites him with an improper invitation:
"Stay here, Noble One! Enjoy yourself, Noble One! I shall attend upon you; I will give you a female slave and a female servant.
Then, it occurs to the monk who has entered the rains retreat: "I have entered the rains retreat in this residence. This..."

And a paṇḍaka approached me and invited me with an improper invitation: "Stay, noble sir! Enjoy yourself, noble sir! I will attend to you; I will give you a female slave and a laborer. [He thought: "If I were to dwell in this residence for the rains, it would lead to an obstacle to my life, an obstacle to my state as a śramaṇa, and an obstacle to my holy life."
"What if I were to depart from this residence? He departs from that residence. Making this very condition his reason, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains retreat.
Var-v § 2.1.7: For example, when a monk who has entered the rains retreat sees a certain young woman of beautiful appearance and lovely form, he grasps at signs in an improper manner (*ayoniśas*).
Then, that monk who has entered the rains retreat thinks: "I have entered the rains retreat in this residence;
and by me, having seen a certain young woman of beautiful appearance and lovely form, a sign was grasped in an improper manner."

It has been taken up. "If I were to dwell in this residence for the rains, it might result in an obstacle to my life, an obstacle to my state of a recluse, or an obstacle to my holy life (brahmacarya). What if I were to depart from this residence? He departs from that residence. On account of this very reason, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains retreat.
Var-v § 2.1.8: Furthermore, it may happen that they point out a hidden treasure to a monk who has entered the rains retreat.

Then, that monk who has entered the rains retreat thinks: "I have entered the rains retreat in this residence, yet they are pointing out this very treasure to me. If I were to remain in this residence for the rains, there might be a threat to my life on account of this."
"The obstacle to the state of a recluse is an obstacle to the holy life. Suppose I were to depart from this residence.
He departs from that residence. Making this very circumstance the reason, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains retreat.
Var-v § 2.1.9: Furthermore, when a monk has entered the rains retreat, his relatives approach him and invite him with an improper invitation:
"Why, Noble One, do you go from house to house with shaven head and bowl in hand? These cool saffron robes of yours distress your body. Come, Noble One; sit down and enjoy sensual pleasures."
...and enjoy [them], give gifts, and perform meritorious deeds. There, a monk who has entered the rains retreat thinks:
"I have entered the rains retreat in this residence, and these relatives of mine, having approached me, invite me with an improper invitation."

"Noble one, why are you shaven-headed, with a bowl in hand, wandering from house to house? And these cool saffron robes of yours distress your body. Come, noble one; sit down, enjoy sensual pleasures, give gifts, and perform meritorious deeds. For my part, I shall dwell in this residence for the rains."

"Because of this, there might be an obstacle to my life, an obstacle to my state of a recluse, or an obstacle to my holy life. Suppose I were to depart from this residence. If he departs from that residence, making this very reason his motive, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains retreat.
Var-v § 2.2.0.2 – (Chinese only) Var-v § 2.2.0.3 – (Chinese only) Var-v § 2.2.0.4 – (Chinese only)
Var-v § 2.2.0.5 – (Chinese only) Var-v § 2.2.0.6 – (Chinese only) Var-v § 2.2.1.a Just as when a king, having equipped his fourfold army— namely, the elephant corps and the cavalry...

The body of chariots and the body of infantry came as far as the gate of the monastery and proclaimed the seizure, saying: "Seize, sirs, the Śākya-son monks! [The rest] is to be recited in detail just as in the *Pravāraṇāvastu*.
Thereupon, it occurred to a monk who had entered the rains retreat in that residence: "I have entered the rains retreat in this residence."

And this king, having mobilized his fourfold army—as previously described—[thinks]: "If I were to spend the rains retreat in this residence, it might lead to an obstacle to my life, an obstacle to my state of a recluse, or an obstacle to my holy life.
What if I were to depart from this residence? He then departs from that residence; this is the very reason.
Having done so, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains-retreat.
Furthermore, it may be that a monk has entered the rains retreat in dependence upon a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka;
he is then seized by a king, or bound, or executed; or his property is confiscated, or he flees to another kingdom or foreign territory out of fear of the king.

Or he has died after having been expelled. In that case, a monk who has entered the rains retreat thinks to himself: "The woman, man, or paṇḍaka upon whom I relied when entering the rains retreat in this residence has been seized by the king, or bound, or executed, or his property has been confiscated."

"Or having fled to another kingdom or another territory out of fear of the king, or having been cut off, he has passed away. If I were to spend the rains retreat in this residence, it might lead to an obstacle to my life, an obstacle to my state of a recluse, or an obstacle to my holy life. What if I were to depart from this residence? He [departed] from there.
If one departs from the residence, making this very circumstance the reason, there is no offense regarding the interruption of the rains retreat.

Furthermore, it may happen that thieves, having committed a raid on a village, a city, or a district, come to the gate of a monastery; having slaughtered a cow, a buffalo, or a goat, and having smeared their limbs with blood and made streaks of blood, they dispatch a messenger to the monks.
"May the noble ones depart;

we shall stay here. Then, while that monk has entered the rains retreat in that residence, the thought occurs to him: "I have entered the rains retreat in this residence, and these bandits, having committed a raid on the village... [as before] ...until he departs from that residence.
Having made this very condition, there is no offense in cutting short the rainy season retreat.
Furthermore, it may be that a monk has entered the rains retreat in dependence upon a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka;
he is then captured by thieves, or bound, or killed,
or his property and wealth is stolen from him.

Or, having fled to another kingdom or another territory out of fear of thieves, or having been cut off, he has passed away. While the monk has been dwelling there for the rains retreat, the thought occurs to him: "In this residence, depending upon a woman, a man, or a *paṇḍaka*, I entered the rains retreat; that person has been seized by thieves, bound, or killed."
"Either his wealth has been seized,

or he has fled to another kingdom or foreign territory out of fear of thieves, or having been ruined, he has passed away. If I were to dwell in this residence during the rains retreat, it might lead to an obstacle to my life."
This is an obstacle to the state of a recluse, an obstacle to the holy life. "What if I were to depart from this residence? He departs from that residence.
Making this very circumstance the reason, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains retreat.
Furthermore, it may happen that some elder who is foolish, deluded, unlearned, and unskilled,

while in a village or on the path to a village, either reviles, addresses, or touches a woman of good family or a maiden of good family. Then people, becoming enraged, come to the gate of the monastery and raise a cry for justice as if they were seizing a criminal.
As before, up until he departs from that residence; making this very circumstance the reason, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains-retreat.
Furthermore, it may be that a monk has entered the rains retreat in dependence upon a woman,
a man, or a paṇḍaka, and he is seized by people, or bound, or killed,
or his property is stolen.

Or, having fled to another kingdom or another territory out of fear of humans, or having been cut off [from his community], he has passed away. While that monk has been dwelling there for the rains-retreat, the thought occurs to him: "The woman, man, or paṇḍaka upon whom I relied when entering the rains-retreat in this residence has been seized or bound by men, or killed, or his property has been confiscated."

Or, having fled to another kingdom or another territory out of fear of humans, he has died after being cut off. "If I were to spend the rains retreat in this dwelling, it might lead to an obstacle to my life, an obstacle to my state of a recluse, or an obstacle to my holy life. What if I were to depart from this dwelling? Thus, he departed from that place.
If he departs from his residence, making this very circumstance the reason, there is no offense regarding the interruption of the rains retreat.
Var-v § 2.2.4.a: For example, suppose a monastery has been established in a region inhabited by non-human beings.

And suppose some senior monk—being foolish, deluded, ignorant, unskilled, and lacking discernment—discharges excrement or urine in an unsuitable place, as described previously, until he departs from that residence. On account of this very circumstance, there is no offense regarding the interruption of the rains retreat.
Furthermore, it may be that a monk has entered the rains retreat depending upon a woman,
a man, or a paṇḍaka, and that person is seized, bound, or killed by non-human beings, or their property is stolen,
or they have fled to another kingdom or foreign territory out of fear of non-human beings.

Or he has died after departing. In that case, it occurs to a monk who has entered the rains retreat: "The woman, man, or paṇḍaka upon whom I relied when entering the rains retreat in this residence has been seized, bound, or killed by non-human beings, or his property has been stolen."

Or, having fled to another kingdom or another territory due to fear of non-human beings, or having been uprooted [from his home], he has passed away. "If I were to dwell in this residence for the rains, there might arise for me, on that account, an obstacle to life, an obstacle to the state of a recluse, or an obstacle to the holy life. What if I were to depart from this residence? Thus, he departed from that place.
If he departs from his residence, making this very circumstance the reason, there is no offense regarding the interruption of the rains retreat.
Furthermore, it may happen that a monastery has been established in a region inhabited by wild beasts.
And some elder— foolish, deluded, ignorant, unskilled, and incompetent— has discharged feces, urine, spittle, snot, vomit, or purgings in an unsuitable place.

Or if the bedding and seating are defiled by impurities and strewn about; or if fierce beasts, being enraged, stay within the range [of the monastery], on the path of the range, on the walking-path (*caṅkrama*), at the fence, or even in the gateway chamber, and they even enter upon the monks. Then, for a monk who has entered the rains-retreat, the thought occurs as before, up until he departs from that residence. Making this very circumstance the reason, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains-retreat.
Furthermore, it may be that a monk has entered the rains retreat depending upon a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka;
he is then seized by wild beasts, or bound, or killed,
or flees to another kingdom or another territory out of fear of wild beasts.

Or he has died after being cut off. In that case, a monk who has entered the rains retreat thinks: "The woman, man, or paṇḍaka upon whom I relied when entering the rains retreat in this residence has been bound by wild beasts, or captured, or his property has been stolen."

Or, having fled to another kingdom or another territory out of fear of wild beasts, or having been cut off and died; "If I were to dwell in this residence for the rains, it would result in an obstacle to my life, an obstacle to my state of a recluse, and an obstacle to my holy life. Thinking, "I shall depart from this residence," he departs from that residence. Making this very circumstance the reason, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains retreat.

Furthermore, as for the case where a monastery has been established in a region inhabited by *nāgas*: as previously described, up until the point that he departs from that residence—making this very circumstance the basis, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains retreat.
Furthermore, it may be that a monk who has entered the rains retreat in reliance upon a woman, a man,
or a paṇḍaka is seized by nāgas, or bound, or killed,
or his personal property is stolen.
Or, having fled to another kingdom or another territory out of fear of *nāgas*, or having been cut off [from his community], he has passed away. Then, a monk who has entered the rains retreat thinks:
"In this residence, depending upon which woman, man, or *paṇḍaka* I entered the rains retreat,"
"He has been seized by nāgas, or bound, or killed, or his wealth and property have been taken away;
or, out of fear of nāgas, he has fled to another kingdom or another territory, or having been uprooted, he has passed away. If I were to spend the rains retreat in this residence..."
"Because of this cause, there might be an obstacle to my life, an obstacle to my state of a recluse, or an obstacle to my holy life.
What if I were to depart from this residence? If he departs from that residence, making this very reason his motive, there is no offense regarding the interruption of the rains retreat.

Furthermore, it may be that a monastery has been established in the middle of a forest. As before, up until he departs from that residence; making this very circumstance the reason, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains retreat.
Furthermore, it may be that the monk who has entered the rains retreat in reliance upon a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka is burned by fire,
or their property is burned by fire.
Or, having fled to another kingdom or another territory due to fear of fire, or having been cut off and passed away; in that case, a monk who has entered the rains retreat thinks:
"In this residence, depending upon which woman, man, or paṇḍaka I have entered the rains retreat,"
He was consumed by fire;
or his wealth and property were consumed by fire;
or, out of fear of fire, he fled to another kingdom or another territory.

Or he has died after cutting himself off. "If I were to spend the rains retreat in this residence, it would lead to an obstacle to my life, an obstacle to my state of a recluse (śrāmaṇya), and an obstacle to my holy life (brahmacarya).
What if I were to depart from this residence? He departs from that residence. Making this very circumstance the reason, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains retreat.

Just as when a monastery has been established in the midst of a marshy area—as previously described—up until the point that he departs from that residence; making this very circumstance the cause, there is no offense regarding the interruption of the rains-retreat.
Furthermore, for example, a monk who has entered the rains retreat depending upon a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, finds that he is swept away by water;
or his property is swept away by water;
or, out of fear of water, he has fled to another kingdom or another territory.

Or he has died after being swept away. In that case, a monk who has entered the rains retreat thinks: "The woman, man, or paṇḍaka upon whom I relied when entering the rains retreat in this residence has been swept away by water; or his property has been swept away by water; or, out of fear of water, he has fled to another kingdom or foreign territory;
or he has been swept away or has died. If I were to stay for the rains in this residence, it might lead to an obstacle to my life."
The obstacle to the state of a recluse is an obstacle to the holy life. "What if I were to depart from this residence?
He departs from that residence. Making this very circumstance the reason, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains retreat.
Var-v § 3 Summary Verse (uddāna):
There is no offense if, through living together and having given a promise... [as previously stated] ...twelve [years] before and twelve after.

Var-v § 3.1.1: Furthermore, it may happen that a monk who has entered the rains retreat sees another monk who, in such and such a manner, commands, persuades, instructs, and trains [others] so as to strive for a schism in the Saṃgha. It is possible that within that very residence, during that same rainy season, the Saṃgha will be split.
In that regard, a monk who has entered the rains retreat thinks: "I have entered the rains retreat in this residence.

Yet this monk is thus commanding, persuading, instructing, and exhorting another monk, striving for a schism in the Saṅgha. It is possible that within this very residence, during this very rainy season, the Saṅgha will be split."
If I were to dwell in this residence for the rains,
it is possible that there might be an obstacle for me in attaining what has not yet been attained,
or in realizing what has not yet been realized.

"For the sake of realizing that which has not yet been realized: 'What if I were to depart from this residence?'—if he departs from that residence making this very reflection his motive, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains-retreat.

Var-v § 3.1.2: Furthermore, it may happen that a monk who has entered the rains-retreat hears: 'In such-and-such a residence, a monk is instructing, persuading, training, and exhorting another monk in such-and-such a manner, striving for the schism of the Saṃgha.'"

It is possible that during the rainy season in that residence the Saṃgha will be split. That monk is one with whom I converse, one with whom I talk, one who is well-acquainted with me, and one who is affectionate toward me. If I were to go there...

Just as in that residence, during this very rainy season, the Saṃgha is not to be split, so a monk must go for seven days, having made a formal determination (*adhiṣṭhāya*), for the sake of a duty of the Saṃgha. If he goes there, it is well;
if he does not go, he incurs an offense. If, having gone there, the seven days have elapsed, there is no offense in the interruption of the rains-retreat.

Var-v § 3.1.3: Furthermore, it may happen that a monk who has entered the rains retreat hears: "In such-and-such a residence, a monk is instructing, persuading, training, and striving for the schism of the Saṃgha in such-and-such a manner.
It is possible that during the rains retreat in that residence, the Saṃgha will split. [Thinking: "That monk is not mine..."

One who is conversant, one who has spoken together, one who is well-acquainted, and one who is affectionate. Moreover, for whomsoever that monk is conversant, with whom he has spoken together, who is well-acquainted, and toward whom he is affectionate—for me, too, that monk is conversant, with whom I have spoken together, who is well-acquainted, and toward whom I am affectionate. If I were to go there...

In such a way that the Saṃgha in that very residence does not split during this very rainy season, a monk should go for seven days after having made a formal determination (adhiṣṭhāya) for the sake of a business of the Saṃgha. If he goes, it is so;
if he does not go, he incurs an offense (sātisāra).
If, having gone there, the seven days have elapsed, [he must return].
There is no offense in the interruption of the rains-retreat.

Var-v § 3.2.1: For example, a monk makes a promise: "I shall dwell for the first three-month period in such-and-such a residence; in those two residences, there shall be a single acquisition and separate *poṣadha* ceremonies. It occurs to him: "While I am dwelling here, it is the same [as there];
while I am dwelling there, it is the same [as here]. Having made this promise, he does not go. Consequently, the first three-month period is not reckoned for him in that residence.
And [an offense] is committed through a promise (*pratiśrava*).
As it is said in the *Varṣāvastu* (§ 3.2.2): "In this case, a monk makes a promise:

'I shall dwell for the preceding three-month period in such-and-such residence. Having made that promise, he departs. Having gone there, he does not accept the voting-slips (*śalākā*) and so forth. For him, the preceding three-month period in that residence is not recognized."
And [an offense] is committed through a promise (*pratiśrava*).
As it is said in the *Varṣāvastu* (Var-v § 3.2.3): "In this case, a monk makes a promise: 'I shall dwell for the preceding three-month period in such-and-such a residence.
Having made that promise, he departs. Having gone there, he accepts the voting-slips (*śalākā*) and so forth, but he does not accept bedding and seating (*śayanāsana*)."
He goes away on business. For him, the previous three-month period in that residence is not reckoned, and by his promise, there is an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
Varṣā-v § 3.2.4: It may be that a monk makes a promise, thinking, "I shall dwell in such-and-such a residence for the first three months of the rains.
Having made this promise, he departs. Having gone there, he takes up the voting sticks and so forth, and he takes up his bedding and seats.
But having entered the rains retreat, he departs on some business. For him, the first three months of the rains in that residence are not accounted as fulfilled.
And by making a promise, one commits a misdeed.

Var-v § 3.2.5: It may happen that a monk makes a promise: "I shall dwell for the preceding three-month period in such-and-such a residence. Having made this promise, he departs. Having gone there, he receives the voting sticks (*śalākā*) and so forth; he takes possession of the bedding and seats.
Having entered the rainy season retreat, he goes outside the boundary for seven days on some business without having formally authorized his departure. In that case, regarding him...
If the prior three-month period in the residence is not known,
there is a *duṣkṛta* offense for making a formal promise.

Varṣā-v § 3.2.6: Furthermore, it may happen that a monk makes a promise, saying, "I shall dwell for the prior three-month period in such-and-such a residence. Having made this promise, he departs. Having gone there, he receives the voting-slips (*śalākā*) and so forth; he takes possession of the bedding and seats.
Having entered the rains-retreat, he goes outside the boundary for seven days on some business without having formally authorized his absence. In that case, regarding him...

If one does not know of the prior three-month period regarding the residence, and there was a verbal agreement [to stay], it is a *duṣkṛta*. If, due to necessary duties, seven days have elapsed [thereby] cutting short the rains retreat, there is no offense.
The six duties should be performed in this manner.
Just as it was during the previous three-month period, so too [was it] during the subsequent one.
The three-month period.
The Chapter on the Rainy Season Retreat is completed.
